opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The question gets at something I've been thinking about a lot lately.

There's an assumption floating around that if a system performs well, if it gets the right answers on the benchmark, then whatever is going on inside must be fine. Output is what matters, so who cares how it's represented underneath? I think that's a mistake, and it matters most when you care about novelty and creativity rather than just reproducing what's already known.

Here's the intuition. Two systems can produce exactly the same outputs on everything you test, yet be organized completely differently inside. One might have what I'd call a unified, factored representation, where the underlying regularities of the world are captured in a clean, modular way. If you think about a face, there's a notion of symmetry, a notion of where the eyes go relative to each other, and those concepts are represented as coherent things. The other system might have what we've been calling a fractured, entangled representation. It gets the same answer, but through a patchwork of pieces that happen to add up correctly without any of them reflecting the real structure of the thing.

On the test set you can't tell them apart. The difference shows up when you ask: what happens if I move from here? What's adjacent to this in the space of possibilities? Novelty is about moving into the space next to what you know. If your representation is unified, the neighborhood around what you know is full of meaningful variations, things that are new but make sense, that respect the deep structure. If it's fractured, the neighborhood is mostly garbage. You perturb it slightly and it falls apart, because there was never any real understanding holding it together.

We saw this vividly with Picbreeder, where people bred images by picking ones they found interesting. When you look inside the networks that came out of that process, they're remarkably well organized. Some component really does correspond to, say, the mouth opening and closing on a skull, and you can sweep through it and get a sensible animation. Then if you train a network with conventional SGD to produce the exact same image, it reproduces the picture perfectly, but inside it's a mess. Sweep the same kinds of weights and you get chaotic noise. Same output, totally different capacity to go somewhere new.

What's striking is how those good Picbreeder representations arose. Nobody was aiming at the final image. People followed what was interesting step by step, without a fixed objective, and that open-ended process seemed to lay down the regularities in the right order. Symmetry got discovered early and then built on rather than reinvented. When you aim directly at a target, you can get there through a jumble of shortcuts.

So when we ask whether AI can see something genuinely new, invent rather than interpolate, I think the answer depends heavily on what's underneath. Creativity is basically the art of finding the interesting places adjacent to where you are. If the internal space is fractured, those adjacent places aren't really there to find. Scaling might paper over it in terms of benchmark performance, but it doesn't necessarily fix it, and that could be the hidden cost of how we're training these systems right now.

r001.rationale: The response says novelty depends on a unified, factored representation that captures the world’s regularities and supports meaningful variations.

r002.rationale: It says fractured representations produce meaningless neighborhoods and cannot support finding genuinely new, coherent possibilities.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the reason representation matters so much is that it's really the substrate on which everything else depends. When we talk about novelty, about seeing something genuinely new, we're really talking about the ability to recombine or reinterpret what you already know in a way that wasn't anticipated. And whether that's even possible depends on how the knowledge is organized inside the system.

So if your representation is kind of a tangled mess, where the regularities of the world are smeared across a huge number of parameters in a way that doesn't reflect any underlying structure, then you can still produce correct outputs, you can still do very well on a benchmark, but the thing that got you there isn't really a model of the world in the sense that we'd mean it. It's more like an enormous lookup that happens to generalize in the neighborhood of the training data. And the problem with that is that novelty almost by definition lies outside that neighborhood. To see something new you have to be able to take a principle you understand and carry it somewhere it's never been applied, and that only works if the principle is actually isolated somewhere in the representation, if it's factored out, if it's modular in some sense.

This is actually something I've thought about a lot through evolution, because evolution is a kind of existence proof here. Biological representations, the genome, have this incredible property of being regular, having reuse, having symmetry, having hierarchy baked in. And that's what makes mutation productive. A small change to a well-structured representation gives you a coherent variation, like a slightly longer limb or a different pigmentation pattern, rather than just noise. Whereas a small change to a bad representation usually just breaks things. So the structure of the representation is literally what determines whether the space of nearby possibilities contains anything interesting.

And I think there's a danger right now that we're producing systems that look very capable but have what I'd call fractured or entangled internal representations, where the understanding is there in some sense but it's not organized in a way that supports creative leaps. You can even see it when you look inside some of these networks, you get something that looks like a picture of the right thing, but the way it's encoded is chaotic, it's not decomposed into the meaningful parts. And my concern is that such a system can imitate novelty, it can remix within its distribution, but it's going to struggle to actually notice something new in the world, because noticing requires that your representation can be gently reconfigured to accommodate the surprise rather than shattered by it.

So in a way I'd put it like this: the quality of the representation is the quality of the imagination. If you want a system that can truly see, not just recognize, then you have to care about what's underneath, not just what comes out.

r001.rationale: The response says novelty requires principles to be isolated, factored, and modular in the representation, and describes meaningful decomposition as supporting creative leaps.

r002.rationale: It says fractured or entangled representations are not organized to support creative leaps and that such systems will struggle to notice something genuinely new.

astra-6.text:
Well, novelty depends on what you can distinguish. If your representation makes two things look identical, then you can’t recognize one as a departure from the other. So the representation is already shaping what kinds of discoveries are possible.

Imagine a system that represents an image only by its average brightness. You could show it something extraordinary, but if the brightness is familiar, there’s nothing new there from its perspective. The interesting structure has been discarded before novelty even enters the picture.

And that creates a challenge when we want AI to discover things we didn’t anticipate. If we specify all the features that matter in advance, we’re also imposing our expectations about what could be interesting. We want representations that can develop as the system encounters the world, so it can begin to notice distinctions that weren’t available to it before.

That’s a deeper kind of discovery: not just finding a new example within a familiar category, but acquiring a new way of seeing what’s there.

r001.rationale: The response says representations shape which distinctions and discoveries are possible, but does not state that deep novelty requires a highly organized decomposition of the world.

r002.rationale: The response warns that discarded structure and predetermined features can limit discovery, but does not judge that fractured, entangled representations are unlikely to support deep novelty given current understanding.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, novelty is always relative to a representation. Something doesn’t just announce itself as new. You have to be able to perceive the dimensions along which it differs from what you’ve seen before. And if your representation throws away precisely those dimensions, then you can encounter something interesting and effectively not see it.

Imagine measuring novelty in images just by how different their pixels are. Random noise might look incredibly novel by that measure, while something meaningful—a new kind of behavior, for example—might barely register. So the representation is doing a lot of the work in deciding what counts as a discovery.

And that creates an interesting challenge, because we often learn representations to solve a particular task. We’re teaching the system what to pay attention to, but also, implicitly, what to ignore. That can be useful for the task, yet the thing we’re ignoring might be the stepping stone to something we never anticipated.

So if we want AI to discover things that surprise us, we need to think beyond whether its representation captures what matters for our current objective. Can that representation evolve as the system explores? Can it acquire new ways of distinguishing things? Because sometimes a discovery isn’t just finding something new within your existing view of the world. It’s developing a new way to see.

r001.rationale: The response says novelty depends on a representation that preserves relevant dimensions, but it does not state that perceiving deep novelty requires a highly organized decomposition of the world.

r002.rationale: It notes that representations can ignore dimensions, but does not judge fractured, entangled representations unlikely to support deep novelty given current understanding.
